title: Northern Greek: the dialects that swallow their vowels
status: Widely heard, mostly as accents and features
lead: Listen to an old shepherd from Roumeli or Thessaly and you may hear **«ου Νίκους πήγι στου χουράφ'»** for **«ο Νίκος πήγε στο χωράφι»**. That is the northern vowel system: unstressed **ι** and **ου** disappear, and unstressed **ε** and **ο** rise to **ι** and **ου**. It covers almost all of mainland Greece north of the Gulf of Corinth, plus Euboea, Lesbos, Samos, the northern Sporades and, until 1922, much of the Asia Minor and East Thracian coast. Since the 19th century the north has been the Greek mainland's great meeting place: Vlachs, Arvanites, Slavic speakers, Sephardic Jews, Turks and, after 1922, hundreds of thousands of refugees from Asia Minor and the Pontus. Northern features are still the most recognisable regional accent in Greece, from the dark **λ** of Thessaloniki to the famous **«σε λέω»**.
facts: From the north shore of the Gulf of Corinth to the northern border: Central Greece (Roumeli), Epirus (except Thesprotia), Thessaly, Macedonia, Thrace, Euboea, Lesbos, Lemnos, Samos, Imbros, Samothrace, the northern Sporades; parts of Andros and Tinos; before 1922 north-west Asia Minor, East Thrace and the Propontis.
Georgios Hatzidakis, who first divided Greek dialects into northern and southern by their vowels.
Skyros, Mykonos, Kastoria, Lefkada, Naousa, Lefkes on Paros, Vourbiani in Epirus, eastern East Thrace, Artaki, Livisi.
Thessaly and Arta 1881; Macedonia, Epirus and the north-eastern Aegean 1912–13; Western Thrace 1920.
Full dialects survive among older villagers; features such as **σε λέω** and the dark **λ** are widespread in everyday speech.

sections.h: Where the northern vowels come from
sections.text:
Nobody knows exactly when northern vowel reduction began. It is not ancient and is not clearly attested in Byzantine texts; it is usually placed in the late medieval or Ottoman period. Hatzidakis explained it by a strong **stress accent**: the stressed syllable was pronounced so forcefully that the unstressed ones shrank or vanished. Later scholars such as Symeonidis and Synodinou refined the idea, but the basic explanation is still accepted.

The north's history explains the rest. Ottoman Rumelia was a land of mixed villages. Greek lived beside Aromanian (Vlach), Albanian, Slavic, Turkish and, in Thessaloniki, the Judaeo-Spanish of the Sephardic Jews who arrived after 1492. When the north joined Greece between 1881 and 1920, and then received the refugees of 1922–23, the old dialects met Pontic, Cappadocian and Asia Minor Greek. In Macedonia and Thrace, refugee speech and local speech blended under the growing influence of Standard Greek.

timeline.text: No clear sign yet of northern vowel loss in the written record.
Ottoman Rumelia: Greek in contact with Aromanian, Albanian, Slavic, Turkish and Judaeo-Spanish. Northern vocalism spreads across the mainland and to the Asia Minor coast.
Thessaly, then Macedonia, Epirus and Thrace join Greece.
The population exchange: more than a million refugees, many of them settled in Macedonia and Thrace.
Thessaloniki's urban speech keeps a few northern traits, which Greeks immediately recognise.

sections.after: **Strict** northern dialects do both things: drop **ι, ου** and raise **ε, ο**. **Semi-northern** dialects usually only drop final **ι** (and often unstressed **ι, ου** inside words) without raising; in Naousa it is the reverse. In Amfissa the raised vowels stop half-way, between [e] and [i].

ο πατέρας μου, ο δικός μου

head: Feature
Northern
Standard
rows: Incomplete synizesis: [j] before stressed **α** sounds like open **ε**
Stress on the fourth syllable from the end

head: Feature
Northern
Standard
rows: Masculine article **ου** (Central Greece, Euboea, Epirus, western Macedonia) or **η** (central and eastern Macedonia, Lesbos, Thessaly)

sections.text: The best-known northern feature is syntactic. Where the standard uses a **genitive** for the person you say or give something to (**σου λέω**, **του το είπα**), northern speakers use the **accusative**, as do the Asia Minor dialects. It is so recognisable that it shapes how other Greeks judge northern speakers, and Thessalonians use it proudly.

examples.en: I told you not to go.

notes: **Skyros**: nouns in **-ος** end in **-ες** (**ο άντζελες**, 'the angel'), **τσαι** for **και**, and **είντα** for 'what'.
**Mykonos**: **κ** as [tʃ] and **γκ** as [dʒ], aorists in **-ξα** (**να σε ρωτήξω κάτι;**), and pronouns after the verb (**δεν έχομέ τις** 'we don't have them').
**East Thrace**: **γ** before initial vowels (**γηύρε** 'he found'), **τις** for masculine 'them' (**τις στόχ'σα** 'I forgot them'), **εκάνανα** for **έκαναν**.

**Livisi** (Lycia): raising without vowel loss, **η αγιασμέ** 'holy water', **έκουσα** 'I heard', **αφεντάδοι** 'masters'. Its people moved to Greece in 1923; the abandoned town (Kayaköy) inspired Louis de Bernières's novel «Birds Without Wings».

listen.intro: The **Vallahades** were Greek-speaking Muslims of the Grevena area in western Macedonia. In 1923 the exchange of populations sent them to Turkey; the village of **Mursallı** has been home since then to families from Gublar (today Μυρσίνη). Their Greek kept the northern vowel system: unstressed **ε → ι**, **ο → ου**, and unstressed **ι, ου** dropped (πουλιά → πλια, κοιμήσου → κμήσ'). Recordings from the VLACH archive of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, played from its YouTube channel and not stored in the app.

cues.el: Μι μουλουγούσι δέδες στου Γκουμπλάρ:
cues.tr: Mi muluɣúɕi dédes stu Gublár:
cues.en: My grandfather from Gublar (Myrsini) told me:

cues.el: Ήταν τσουτσανός.
cues.tr: Ítan ʨuʨanós.
cues.en: Once there was a boy.

cues.el: Λέει η μάνα τ': «Σιλιμάν», λε, «ιγώ θα πάνου σ' κουμπσίσα», λε.
cues.tr: ʎeĭ i mána-t: <Syʎimán,> ʎe, <iɣó θa pánu s kumpɕíɕa,> ʎe.
cues.en: His mother said: <Suleiman, I will go to the neighbour.

cues.el: «Τήρα κουσάρια μι τα πλια», λε,
cues.tr: <Téra kusária mi ta pʎa,> ʎe,
cues.en: Keep an eye on the hen with the chickens,

cues.el: «να μη τα παρ' κανά γιράκ'», λε, «κι να μη τα φάει», λε.
cues.tr: <na mi ta par kaná ʝirák,> ʎe, <kꞌi na mi ta faĭ,> ʎe.
cues.en: so that the hawk will not take and eat them.>

cues.el: Πάει αυτήν σ' γιτουνιά. Αυτός χάλιβι να παίξ'.
cues.tr: Paĭ aftín ʑ-ʝitunǽ. Aftós χáʎivi na pékɕ.
cues.en: She went to the neighbourhood. He wanted to play.

cues.el: Εμ, τώρα να τ' αφήκ', α φύγουν.
cues.tr: Em, tóra na t-afíkꞌ, a fíɣun.
cues.en: But if he leaves them alone, they’ll run away.

cues.el: Του πήρι… τα πήρι τα πλια, πουδάρ' πουδάρ' πουδάρ' τ' άδισι.
cues.tr: Tu píri -- ta píri ta pʎa, puðár puðár puðár t-áðiɕi.
cues.en: So he took the chickens and tied them by their feet.

cues.el: Τ' άδισι κι ν' κουσάρα, πάει να παίξ'.
cues.tr: T-áðiɕi kꞌi ŋ-gusárà, paĭ na pekɕ.
cues.en: He also tied the hen and went to play.

cues.el: Ήρσι του σαχίν, του γιράκ', τα πήρι όλα, έφυι.
cues.tr: Írɕi tu ɕaçíɲ, tu ʝerákꞌ, ta píri óla, éfii.
cues.en: The hawk came, took them all and left.

cues.el: Ήρθι η μάνα τ': «Πού είνι, Σιλιμάν, τα πλια μι ν' κότα;» λε.
cues.tr: Írθi i mána-t: <Pu íɲi, Syʎimán, ta pʎa m-iɲ- góta?> ʎe.
cues.en: His mother came: <Where are the chickens with the hen?>

cues.el: «Τα πήρι, μάνα», λε. Τουν έδιρι μάνα τ'.
cues.tr: <Ta píri, mána,> ʎe. Tun éðiri mána-t.
cues.en: <It took them, mother.> His mother hit him.

cues.el: Αυτός κλαίουντας κλαίουντας πάει στου μύλου.
cues.tr: Aftós kléundas-kʎéundas paĭ stu mílu.
cues.en: Weeping he ran to the mill.

cues.el: Λέει αυτός ι μύλους, μυλουνάς: «Τι κλαις ρα, Σιλιμάν;» λε.
cues.tr: ʎeĭ aftós i míʎus, milunás: <Ti kʎes ra, Syʎimán?> ʎe.
cues.en: The miller asked: <Why are you crying, Suleiman?>

cues.el: «Για», λέει, «πάει η μάνα μ' γιτνιά, έτσας κι έτσας έκαμα
cues.tr: <Ĭa,> ʎeĭ, <paĭ i mána-m ʝityɲá éʨas kꞌ-éʨas ékama
cues.en: <My mother went to the neighbour. This and that happened

cues.el: κι μ' έδιρι», λε.
cues.tr: kꞌi m-édiri,> ʎe.
cues.en: and she hit me.>

cues.el: «Κάτσι ιδώ απόψι», λέει, «κμήσ'. Ιγώ θα φύγου», λε.
cues.tr: <Káʨi iðó apópɕi,> ʎeĭ, <kꞌimís. Iɣó θa fíɣu,> ʎe.
cues.en: <Stay and sleep here tonight. I will go,> he said.

cues.el: Πάει στου μύλου, κμήθκι, ξύπνισι τ' νύχτα, βγήκι όξου.
cues.tr: Paĭ stu mílu, kꞌimíθkꞌi, ɕípɲiɕi t-ɲíχta, víkꞌi óksu.
cues.en: He went to the mill to sleep. In the night he woke up and went out.

cues.el: Άφκι μ' πόρτα ανοιχτή, πάει του γουρούν', ε, τ' όφαϊ τ' αλεύρ'.
cues.tr: Áfk'i ɱ-bórta aɲiχtí, paĭ tu ɣurún, é, t-ófai t- aʎévrꞌ.
cues.en: He left the door open. Then the pig came and ate the flour.

cues.el: Ήρθι τ' χαραΐ μυλουνάς: «Σιλιμάν», λέει, «πού είνι τ' αλεύρ';» λε.
cues.tr: Írθi t-χaraí milunás: <Syʎimán,> ʎeĭ, <pu íɲi t- aʎévrꞌ?> ʎe.
cues.en: At dawn, the miller came back: <Suleiman, where is the flour?>

cues.el: «Τ' όφαϊ του γουρούν'», λε. Τουν έδιρι κι αυτός.
cues.tr: <T-ófaĭ tu ɣurún,> ʎe. Tun édiri kꞌ-aftós.
cues.en: <The pig ate it>. And so, he hit him too.

cues.el: Βγήκι όξου. Βρήκι έναν… Ρουμνιός.
cues.tr: Víkꞌi óksu. Vríkꞌi énàn -- Rumɲós.
cues.en: He went out and found a (Christian) Greek.

cues.el: «Τι κρες ρα, Σιλιμάν;» λε.
cues.tr: <Ti kres ra, Syʎemán?> ʎe.
cues.en: <Why do you cry, Suleiman?> he said.

cues.el: «Έτσ' άιας κι έτσ' άιας», λε, «μ' έδιρι η μάνα μ'», λέει.
cues.tr: <Eʨ áĭas kꞌ-eʨ áĭas,> ʎe, <m-éðiri i mána-m,> ʎeĭ.
cues.en: <This and that happened. My mother hit me,> he said.

cues.el: «Πήγα στου μύλου.
cues.tr: <Píɣa stu mílu.
cues.en: <I went to the mill.

cues.el: Έφαϊ του γουρούν' τ' αλεύρ'», λέει. «Μ' έδιρι κι αυτός», λε.
cues.tr: Éfai tu ɣurún t-aʎévrꞌ,> ʎeĭ. <M-édiri kꞌ-aftós,> ʎe.
cues.en: The pork ate the flour. And that man hit me too.>

cues.el: «Έλα, να σι πάρου ιγώ να γέντσ' θκο μ' πιδί», λε.
cues.tr: <Éla, na ɕi páru iɣó na ĭénʦ θkó-m piðí,> ʎe.
cues.en: <Come, I will take you to become my child.>

cues.el: Γιατί ήταν Ρουμνός. Κλαίουντας πάει πάλι στου σπίτ'.
cues.tr: Ʝatí itan Rumnós. Kʎéundas paĭ páʎi stu ɕpitꞌ.
cues.en: Because he was a Greek. And so he ran back home crying.

cues.el: Δεν πάισι…
cues.tr: Ðen-báĭsi ---.
cues.en: Do not go to ---.

cues.el: Αυτό μι μουλουγούσι.
cues.tr: Aftó mi muluɣúɕi.
cues.en: That is what he told me.

cues.el: Ν' Κυριακή έβαναμι του μπαϊράκ'. Χιρνούσι η χαρά.
cues.tr: Ɲ-g'ir'ák'í évanami tu baĭrák'. Çirnúɕi i χará.
cues.en: On Sunday we put the wedding flag. The marriage started.

cues.el: Μ' Πέφτ' μέρα πήαμ, πάιναμι ταχνά μι του ζγουρ'.
cues.tr: Ɱ-beft' méra píam, páĭnami taçná mi tu ʑɣur.
cues.en: On Thursday morning we went and brought the lamb.

cues.el: Του ζγουρ', τσ' νύφς τα κιαφέτια,
cues.tr: Tu ʑgur, ʦ ɲifs ta kɯafétĭa,
cues.en: The lamb and the bride’s clothes,

cues.el: ταχνά τα πάιναμι.
cues.tr: taçná ta páĭnami.
cues.en: we brought them in the morning.

cues.el: Μας έδουναν ψουμί ικεί, εκάθουμασταν, έτρουγαμι ψουμί.
cues.tr: Mas éðunan psumí ik'i, ekáθumastan, étruɣami psumí.
cues.en: There they gave us bread [food] and we had a meal.

cues.el: Χουσαβέρ γυρνούσαμι, έρουμασταν πάλι ιδώ.
cues.tr: Husavér ʝirnúsami, érumastan páʎi iðó.
cues.en: Then we returned.

cues.el: Του Σάβατου μι ν' Κυριακή έβαναμι τα βιουλιά.
cues.tr: Tu Savátu mi ɲ-g'ir'ak'í évanámi ta vʝuʎá.
cues.en: On Saturday and Sunday the violins [musicians] played.

cues.el: Λαλούσαν, χόριβναν, ίπιναν.
cues.tr: Lalúsan, χórivnan, ípçinan.
cues.en: They played, they danced, they drank.

cues.el: Ν' Κυριακή τ' μέρα ύστιρα μι του κουμβόι πάιναμι να πάρουμι τ' νύφ'.
cues.tr: Ɲ-g'ir'ak'í t-méra íɕtirà mi tu kumvóĭ páĭnami na párumi t-ɲif'.
cues.en: Later on Sunday, we went in a group to take the bride.

cues.el: Ούλου του χουριό, όπιους ήνταν νταβετλής.
cues.tr: Úlu tu χurʝó, ópçus índan dávetʎís.
cues.en: All those invited from the village,

cues.el: Του ν' έκραϊγάν, πάιναν, έπιρναν τ' νύφ'. Έρουμασταν.
cues.tr: Tuɲ-ékraĭɣán, páinan, épirnan t-ɲif'. Érumastan.
cues.en: The guests went to take the bride. We came back.

cues.el: Οι χαρές μας έτσ' γένουνταν.
cues.tr: I χarés mas ĭeʨ ʝénundan.
cues.en: That was how our marriages were.

cues.el: — Τα φαγιά; Τι φαγιά έφκιαναν; — Α, φαγιά:
cues.tr: - Ta faĭá? Tí faĭá éfk'anan? - Á, faĭá:
cues.en: - What kind of food did they make? - Ah, food:

cues.el: Μπακλαβάν έφκιαναμι, φασούλια, μουσακάν, τσουρβάν, ριζ, κιμπάπ.
cues.tr: Ɱbaklaván éfk'anami, fasúʎa, musakán, ʨurván, riʑ, k'ibáp.
cues.en: We made baklava, beans, moussaka, soup, rise, kebab.

cues.el: — Πίτις; — Πίτις έφκιαναμι, μπιρέκια.
cues.tr: - Pítis? - Pítis éfk'anami, birék'a.
cues.en: - Pies? - We made pies, bourek.

cues.el: — Ύστιρα κι μουσακά. — Ναι, είπεν για μουσακά. Άμα…
cues.tr: - Ístira ki musaká. - Ne, ípen ʝa musaká. Áma --
cues.en: - Finally, moussaka. - Yes, he mentioned moussaka. But --

cues.el: — Μι πράσα μουσακά.
cues.tr: - Mi prása musaká.
cues.en: - Moussaka with leek.

cues.el: — Νύφις παλιά πέρναν κι από άλλα χουριά;
cues.tr: - Nífis paʎá pérnan k'-apo ála χurʝá?
cues.en: - But did you marry brides from other villages?

cues.el: — Έρουνταν, έπερναν. — Έπερναν κι από χριστιανό;
cues.tr: - Érundan, épernan. - Épernan k'i apó χristĭanó?
cues.en: - Yes, we did. - Also from Christians?

cues.el: — Όχι, όχι. — Δεν έπερναν. Τώρα πέρουν. Τώρα…
cues.tr: - Óçi, óçi. - Ðen épernan. Tóra pérun. Tóra ---
cues.en: - No, no. - They didn’t. But now they do.

cues.el: — Αρβανίτ', μι τσ' αρβανίτ', πρώτα δεν είχαμε τέτοιο.
cues.tr: - Arvanít, mi ts-arvanít, próta ðen éxame tétço.
cues.en: - Before, we didn’t even mix with the Albanians.

cues.el: Τώρα, τώρα το ίρχισαν.
cues.tr: Tóra, tóra to írçisan.
cues.en: Now they’ve started to.

cues.el: — Εδώ στου χουριό, στου Μουρσαλί; — Έβετ, έβετ.
cues.tr: - Eðó stu χurʝó, stu Mursalɯ? - Évet, évet.
cues.en: - Here in the village, in Mursallı? - Yes, yes.

culture.text: In Thessaloniki, the dark **λ** and **σε λέω** are part of local identity, celebrated in comedy and songs. In Epirus, the polyphonic songs of Pogoni and Zagori, and in Thessaly and Roumeli the **κλέφτικα** songs of the mountain fighters, keep old northern pronunciations alive. Many northern families also remember Pontic, Cappadocian or Asia Minor grandparents, so a single village may hold several dialects at once.

questions.q: «Ου Νίκους» is the northern form of…
questions.why: Unstressed **ο** rises to **ου** in the article and in the ending.

questions.q: Who first divided Greek dialects into northern and southern?
questions.why: He noticed the different vowel systems.
Northern Greek uses the accusative for the indirect object.
Skyros, Mykonos, Kastoria and Lefkada drop some unstressed vowels but do not raise ε and ο.
